title: A solitary extraventricular subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in the absence of tuberous sclerosis
case_prompt:
A 17-year-old boy presented with new-onset seizures characterized by focal motor activity of the right upper and lower extremities with secondary generalization. He was otherwise healthy, with no family history of seizures or tuberous sclerosis, and reported no other symptoms. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and comprehensive metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Neurologic examination revealed no focal deficits. Electroencephalography in awake and drowsy states, as well as during photic stimulation and hyperventilation, was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a 1.8 × 2.4 × 2.2 cm mass in the subcortical and deep white matter and adjacent cortex of the left occipital lobe. On T2-weighted images, the lesion was predominantly hypointense with internal linear hyperintensities. On T1-weighted images, it showed peripheral mild hyperintensity with a central hypointense core. Susceptibility-weighted imaging revealed marked hypointensity. Postcontrast T1-weighted images disclosed a few small areas of central enhancement, whereas the remainder of the lesion enhanced minimally. No enlarged feeding arteries or draining veins were identified to suggest an arteriovenous malformation. The leading considerations on MRI were cavernous malformation, calcified low-grade tumor, and dystrophic cerebral calcification.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cavernous malformation was suspected based on the pronounced susceptibility hypointensity and lack of vascular flow voids — “Hence, the differential diagnosis on MRI included cavernous malformation, calcified low-grade tumor, and dystrophic cerebral calcification.”  
2. A calcified low-grade tumor was considered given the lesion’s dense calcifications and minimal enhancement — “Hence, the differential diagnosis on MRI included cavernous malformation, calcified low-grade tumor, and dystrophic cerebral calcification.”  
3. Dystrophic cerebral calcification was considered because of the marked hypointense signal on susceptibility-weighted images — “Hence, the differential diagnosis on MRI included cavernous malformation, calcified low-grade tumor, and dystrophic cerebral calcification.”  
4. Other pediatric calcified intra-axial lesions, including ganglioglioma/gangliocytoma, ependymoma, oligodendroglioma, and primitive neuroectodermal tumor, were included in the differential — “Differential considerations for calcified intra-axial supratentorial pediatric lesions include cavernous malformation, ganglioglioma/gangliocytoma, ependymoma, oligodendroglioma, and primitive neuroectodermal tumor.”  
5. Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma was established when pathology demonstrated a markedly calcified glial tumor composed of spindle to giant cells with abundant cytoplasm, hyalinized vessels, and immunopositivity for Olig-2 and GFAP — “These findings were consistent with the diagnosis of subependymal giant cells astrocytoma.”
